Geth EVM memory and host-runtime disassembly
============================================

Purpose
-------
Optimized machine-code disassembly for geth's EVM package, all linked EVM
opcode handlers, the RPC -> state transition -> state read path, and selected
compiled dependencies and Go runtime routines. This is x86-64 assembly emitted
by Go's objdump. It is not EVM bytecode.

Build target and provenance
---------------------------
Source: github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum, branch master snapshot
Source commit: 92cbc7782990381949447f4b07d860e1c239df02 (2026-11-23)
Target OS/architecture: linux/amd64
Host CPU reported by lscpu: Intel Xeon Platinum 8370C
Kernel: Linux 6.8.0-1070-azure
Go compiler: go1.27.3 linux/amd64
Build command: go build -trimpath -buildvcs=false -ldflags=-w -o /tmp/geth-prod-disasm ./cmd/geth
Optimization: normal production compiler settings; no -N/-l debug switches.
DWARF omitted with -w; Go function symbols retained for disassembly.
Disassembler: go tool objdump from the same Go toolchain.

How to read this file
---------------------
Each section has the linked binary's address, machine-code bytes, decoded
x86-64 instruction, and Go source line when available. Addresses are specific
to this build. Compiler inlining and register allocation mean this is one
optimized implementation, not a stable ABI or a one-to-one source translation.

The physical CPU itself has no program disassembly for its cache/RAM layout.
This file shows instructions the geth executable asks the CPU to run. Linux
kernel code is not linked into geth. QEMU and a separately booted Ubuntu Server
guest are documented in the final sections; they are separate programs and
their machine instructions are not part of the geth ELF.

Source references
-----------------
Geth source: https://github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum/tree/92cbc7782990381949447f4b07d860e1c239df02
Linux process address spaces: https://docs.kernel.org/6.15/mm/process_addrs.html
QEMU memory API: https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/devel/memory.html
QEMU translator internals: https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/devel/tcg.html

Sections
--------
1-5. RPC, state, interpreter, EVM memory, and Go runtime sample paths
6. Complete byte-to-handler map for the Bogota instruction table
7. All linked EVM opcode handlers
8. Dynamic gas and memory-size helpers
9. RPC-selected state loading, trie reads, and commit path
10. Go runtime's Linux syscall boundary
11. Complete compiled core/vm package
12. uint256 arithmetic and Keccak dependencies
13. QEMU 8.2.2 memory-region, address-space, and KVM functions
14. Ubuntu Server 24.04.5 guest kernel provenance and disassembly boundary
15. Runtime trace of one local eth_call and separate QEMU/KVM boot

===== 14. Ubuntu Server guest kernel provenance and exact-symbol boundary =====
Official image: Ubuntu Server 24.04.5 live-server-amd64 ISO, /tmp/ubuntu-24.04.5-live-server-amd64.iso. SHA-256 verified against the official SHA256SUMS: 97f3d7ffb032c3eb3b23d2c8be9cc76e60c2c1f2c0146ba5ba9fe01cafae0fd8. This is the Server ISO, not the Desktop GUI image.
Extracted guest kernel: Linux 6.8.0-139-generic, build #139-Ubuntu, x86-64. The extracted /tmp/ubuntu-server-vmlinux is an ELF64 kernel image, Build ID 61e84c0b5c196ad18825c262fa40fc0b00c4ddb8, but it is stripped and has no .symtab. The live installer booted this kernel under the QEMU configuration above.
The guest kernel .BTF section describes types, not executable symbols or instruction bytes. Without the matching Ubuntu kernel debug ELF/System.map, function names such as do_mmap, handle_mm_fault, and alloc_pages cannot be reliably placed in this stripped image, so no guest kernel routine is labeled or claimed here. The host Azure kernel is also a separate binary; this report does not include its KVM implementation.
The observable boundary is: geth instructions call Linux syscalls; QEMU creates guest RAM/address-space regions and registers them with KVM; KVM asks the host kernel to run guest code; guest Linux then handles its own memory syscalls and page faults. Hardware page tables, caches, and DRAM signaling are not themselves disassemblable software layers.
Official references: Ubuntu Server images and checksums at https://releases.ubuntu.com/24.04/ ; QEMU memory model at https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/devel/memory.html ; QEMU load/store access at https://www.qemu.org/docs/master/devel/loads-stores.html .

===== 15. Runtime trace: one local eth_call and its host/VM boundaries =====
This is an observed execution, not a synthetic trace. Geth was built from source commit 92cbc7782990381949447f4b07d860e1c239df02 using the production settings above, then run locally with --dev (chain ID 1337). The trace used a fresh local data directory, block 1, and the Bogota fork active at timestamp zero. This is reproducible evidence for this example only; it is not a claim about a public chain or every eth_call.

Test contract: init code 0x600b600c600039600b6000f360003560005260206000f3. Deployed runtime bytecode: 0x60003560005260206000f3. It reads the first 32 bytes of calldata, stores that word at EVM memory offset 0, then returns 32 bytes.
Deployment transaction: 0x8c94016d4cfe9abe6647ce22009d8eede74cb866dd2f1e59e494fcedbe992983, included in block 1 with status 1 and 0xd8ee gas used.
RPC request: eth_call({from: 0x71562b71999873db5b286df957af199ec94617f7, to: 0x3a220f351252089d385b29beca14e27f204c296a, data: 0x11223344}, latest).
RPC result: 0x1122334400000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000.
Block context: number 1, hash 0x11cf5492441b6dac7f7a319732b300f2a82c89a29f98a867d7c0124f891679bc, state root 0x1e5ae19c4a8c50cb09ad44eb76a9d45b4c831922bf0440f29e668ae935a8bea0, timestamp 0x6b0584db. Chain ID 1337.

Opcode trace (geth debug_traceCall, depth 1; stack shown bottom-to-top as returned by geth):
pc  opcode          gas cost  stack before                                      effect
0   PUSH1           3         []                                               pushes 0x00
2   CALLDATALOAD    3         [0x00]                                           pushes 0x11223344 followed by 28 zero bytes
3   PUSH1           3         [word]                                           pushes 0x00
5   MSTORE          6         [word, 0x00]                                     writes the 32-byte word to EVM memory [0, 32)
6   PUSH1           3         []                                               pushes 0x20
8   PUSH1           3         [0x20]                                           pushes 0x00
10  RETURN          0         [0x20, 0x00]                                     returns memory [0, 32)
Result: success, 7 opcode steps, 21,160 total gas reported by the tracer. The 6 gas at MSTORE includes the first 32-byte memory expansion plus the store. The static handler mapping in section 6 resolves these opcodes to opPush1, opCallDataLoad, opMstore, and opReturn; the corresponding compiled native code is in section 7. An EVM opcode is one VM operation and does not equal one CPU instruction.

State observed by geth's prestateTracer: caller 0x71562b71999873db5b286df957af199ec94617f7 had nonce 1 and balance 0xffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffffd3ce3c332d77. Target 0x3a220f351252089d385b29beca14e27f204c296a had nonce 1, balance 0, code hash 0xcd03839fefd9166b06feeea88c36d6ad42a489791c88cc7a4ba28afbf029a8f0, and the runtime bytecode shown above. The call made no persistent state change. These values came from the local dev chain, not from the contract or this eth_call request.

Host OS boundary for the eth_call: strace recorded 26 syscalls across the geth threads during the 10.5 ms request window. The request arrived on loopback TCP port 18545; geth accepted the socket, read the HTTP/JSON-RPC request, woke a Go worker with futex, wrote HTTP 200 with the result, and closed the connection. Representative events (epoch timestamps are from strace):
1795523847.850205 accept4(84, ..., SOCK_CLOEXEC|SOCK_NONBLOCK) = 83
1795523847.851030 read(83, "POST / HTTP/1.1 ... eth_call ...", 4082) = 306
1795523847.851167 futex(..., FUTEX_WAKE_PRIVATE, 1) = 1
1795523847.851874 write(83, "HTTP/1.1 200 OK ...", 211) = 211
1795523847.853256 epoll_ctl(5, EPOLL_CTL_DEL, 83, ...) = 0
No explicit database file open/read/write syscall appeared in this short request interval. That does not mean geth skipped state access: the database may have served state from memory or an existing mapping, and ordinary mapped-memory loads are not reported as syscalls. This trace does not expose Linux kernel function calls or CPU page faults.

Separate QEMU/KVM runtime observation: during a boot of the same Ubuntu Server ISO, QEMU opened /dev/kvm, issued KVM_CREATE_VM and two KVM_CREATE_VCPU calls, and submitted guest memory with KVM_SET_USER_MEMORY_REGION. The system-call trace recorded 89 KVM_SET_USER_MEMORY_REGION operations and 189,492 KVM_RUN calls during the captured boot interval. The QEMU trace backend recorded 89 kvm_set_user_memory events, 105,408 memory-region reads, and 200,257 memory-region writes, mainly firmware and virtual-device activity. These counters describe the separate ISO boot, not the geth eth_call.
Example initial RAM registration: ioctl(KVM_SET_USER_MEMORY_REGION, {slot=0, guest_phys_addr=0, memory_size=2147483648, userspace_addr=...}) = 0. QEMU subsequently split the map around reserved/read-only regions; for example GPA 0xe0000-0x100000 was a 131,072-byte read-only slot and GPA 0x100000 onward held guest RAM. QEMU event examples include RTC index/data reads and writes and port 0x92 writes during boot.

Runtime trace capture limits: EVM-level execution is traced opcode by opcode. strace observes user-to-kernel calls but does not trace the Linux kernel's internal functions. QEMU's trace events and KVM ioctls are observed in a different boot, not in the same process as geth. No native CPU instruction-by-instruction trace, guest Linux page-fault/function trace, or host KVM kernel function trace was captured. Static machine-code sections remain the way to inspect those compiled routines until matching symbols and kernel tracing access are available.
Raw captures used for this section were written under /tmp/geth-runtime-trace/ (structlog.json, prestate.json, strace.log, qemu.trace, and qemu-syscalls.log); this report retains the representative inputs, outputs, and events in one text file.
